marks: Bonpos hold that Bon was brought first to Zhangzhung, the kingdom around Mount Kailash, and then to Tibet.
Robert Thurman dates a Bon court religion of the Yarlung kings to around 100 BCE, under King Pudegungyal.
Menri, the most important Bon monastery, was built in Tsang in 1405.
Bonpo representatives came to the 14th Dalai Lama here in 1979, and the Central Tibetan Administration accepted Bon as a religious group.
The refounded Menri, Bon’s leading monastery in India, where the successor of Lungtok Tenpai Nyima (1929–2017) presides.
notes: Bonpos hold that Bon came from Olmo Lungring to Zhangzhung and then to Tibet; Robert Thurman dates a Bon court religion of the Yarlung kings to around 100 BCE.
Bon priests serve the royal cult of the early Tibetan Empire; Bon tradition places the Zhangzhung Dzogchen master Tapihritsa in the 7th century.
Under the Buddhist king Trisong Detsen (r. 740–797) Bon declines; Bon histories tell of persecution, and of texts hidden as treasures by masters such as Drenpa Namkha.
Yungdrung Bon takes shape in the 10th and 11th centuries, as treasure revealers such as Shenchen Luga (996–1035) bring out hidden texts.
Loden Nyingpo (1360–1385) reveals the Zibji, and New Bon begins in eastern Tibet.
Menri monastery is built in Tsang (1405); the Bon Kanjur is probably assembled by 1450.
The Fifth Dalai Lama converts some Bon monasteries to the Gelug school by force but officially recognises Bon as a Tibetan religion.
Many Bonpos are executed in the Dzungar invasion of Tibet (1717); New Bon treasures are still revealed in eastern Tibet.
Bon flourishes in eastern Tibet under lamas such as Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen; the canon is carved on woodblocks at Trochu.
China invades Tibet (1950), where there are about 300 Bon monasteries; Bon suffers in the Cultural Revolution, and in exile it is recognised by the Central Tibetan Administration (1979).
Scholars estimate about 400,000 Bonpos on the Tibetan Plateau (2019); Bon monasteries in Tibet have been rebuilt since 1980.
